sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

matches.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. matches.title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. matches.title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
matches.abstract_excerpt: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. Our method is inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN) paradigm, which replaces fixed linear transformations with learnable univariate functions. passages.text: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

The L L -only variant is the S ≡ 0 S\equiv 0 special case of S-SALAAD. It retains ADMM’s coupled updates of X X and L L under the constraint X = L X\!=\!L , with the proximal update ( 8 ) explicitly removing small singular values from L L . This structure-learning procedure goes beyond directly adding a low-rank regularizer to the task loss. Figure 8 compares this variant with direct subgradient optimization of ℓ ⁡ ( X ) + λ ​ | X | ∗ \ell(X)\!+\!\lambda|X|_{*} . With λ = 10 − 6 \lambda\!=\!10^{-6} , perplexity is comparable to that of L L -only S-SALAAD at the largest budget but rises sharply as the budget decreases. This behavior is consistent with low-rank structure that is too weak to support aggressive compression. Increasing λ \lambda to 10 − 5 10^{-5} strengthens rank regularization and yields nearly constant perplexity across the tested budgets, supporting elastic compression at the cost of higher perplexity throughout. L L -only S-SALAAD maintains low perplexity over the same budget range, providing a better trade-off between model quality and elastic compressibility than these direct regularization baselines. Figures 23 and 24 extend the deployment evaluation to an RTX 2080 Ti and 4 × \times AMD EPYC 7662 CPUs. Relative to vanilla inference, block- × 64 64\!\times\!64 S-SALAAD at a 500M budget reduces peak GPU memory usage by 42.4% and achieves 2.25 × 2.25\times throughput on Llama-1B with the RTX 2080 Ti (Figure 23(a) ). For Qwen3-1.7B at 800M, the corresponding gains are 31.5% lower peak GPU memory usage and 1.80 × 1.80\times throughput (Figure 23(b) ). On CPU, these compressed variants reduce peak RAM usage by 61.5% with 2.78 × 2.78\times throughput for Llama-1B (Figure 24(a) ), and by 50.6% with 2.20 × 2.20\times throughput for Qwen3-1.7B (Figure 24(b) ). These results demonstrate that S-SALAAD’s memory and inference gains extend across the evaluated hardware platforms. Detailed numerical results are provided in Appendix H . The deployment conclusions of Sections 5.1 and 5.2 also extend to these settings.

Applying SliceGPT and SVD-LLM to L L -only checkpoints pretrained with S-SALAAD yields lower perplexity at the same inference cost than applying them to vanilla-pretrained checkpoints. This benefit persists on both GPU and CPU (Figures 23(a) and 24(a) ), demonstrating that the learned compressibility remains useful across hardware. Block granularity and deployment trade-offs. On Llama-1B, the × 16 16\!\times\!16 variant achieves lower perplexity than L L -only under tight compression budgets (Figure 6(b) ). Its additional inference overhead, however, limits the deployment gains on both GPU and CPU (Figures 23(a) and 24(a) ). Increasing the block size reduces this overhead, allowing × 64 64\!\times\!64 to closely track the L L -only perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs on the RTX 2080 Ti and improve on them at CPU operating points. These trends support the conclusion that retaining S S can improve deployment trade-offs beyond L L -only when block granularity is matched to the target hardware, as further illustrated in Appendix G .

inspect:2610.30280.question: What transformer or language-model training experiments compare Muon or PolarGD with AdamW or gradient descent, and what measured performance differences and experimental controls support the claimed benefit of Newton–Schulz iterations?

passages.text: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a strong optimizer for training large neural networks. It has matched or outperformed AdamW in language-model pretraining, from speedrun benchmarks ( Jordan et al., 2024a ) to large-scale training ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Shah et al., 2025 ) , and standard optimizers more broadly in vision ( Jordan et al., 2024b ; Pethick et al., 2025 ) , diffusion ( Schaipp, 2025 ) , and tabular models ( Gorishniy et al., 2026 ) . For two-dimensional parameter blocks, Muon approximately orthogonalizes the momentum matrix with a few Newton--Schulz iterations, that is, it steps along an approximation of the polar factor polar ⁡ ( G ) = U ​ V ⊤ \mathrm{polar}(G)=UV^{\top} of G = U ​ Σ G ​ V ⊤ G=U\Sigma_{G}V^{\top} . The same direction is shared by a broader family of matrix optimizers. It is the steepest-descent direction for the spectral norm, used in stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015a ; Carlson et al., 2016 ; Carlson et al., 2015b ) and revisited by Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) . It is also the linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) direction of norm-constrained methods ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) reduces to it when preconditioner accumulation is switched off ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . Controlled benchmarks place such matrix-based optimizers among the strongest available ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , so understanding when a step along polar ⁡ ( G ) \mathrm{polar}(G) helps matters well beyond Muon .

Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) .

inspect:2610.32142.question: In practical LLM fine-tuning, which models, tasks, and baselines are used to compare the proposed initialization with standard LoRA initialization and LoRA+? How do performance and training stability vary across asymmetric learning-rate ratios, with matched tuning and adapter ranks?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix B B than for the down-projection matrix A A . However, the ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal–noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard Init[A] , the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for B B , η B \eta_{B} , the initialization scale β \beta , and the adapter rank r r . In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple initialization that scales the variance of A A as σ A 2 ∝ n − 2 \sigma_{A}^{2}\propto n^{-2} while keeping B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1 / n 1/n , stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, Init[ A

Across tasks and models, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard Init[A] , and makes the width-based guideline η B ≈ n ​ η A \eta_{B}\approx n\eta_{A} a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 22 ] is a standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) [ 21 , 35 , 33 ] . Given a width- n n LoRA layer with pretrained weight W ∈ ℝ n × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and input Z ¯ ∈ ℝ n \underline{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , LoRA uses Z ¯ = W ​ Z ¯ + α r ​ B ​ A ​ Z ¯ \bar{Z}=W\underline{Z}+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\underline{Z} , where A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable with learning rates (LRs) η A \eta_{A} and η B \eta_{B} . Here r ≪ n r\ll n is the adapter rank and α / r \alpha/r is the LoRA update multiplier. inspect:2610.32878.question: At matched parameter or compression budgets, which SVD-based LLM compression baselines are compared with LEMS and KFAC-SVD on Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3? What are the measured perplexity and zero-shot accuracy differences, and how are calibration data, recovery fine-tuning, and model sizes controlled?

passages.text: We evaluate KFAC-SVD against state-of-the-art methods across three LLM families: Mistral , Llama 3 , and Qwen3 . Table 2 details the results for all approaches under uniform compression rates (0.9, 0.7) and calibration sample count, with an additional line for our search-enhanced variant. KFAC-SVD consistently yields the lowest perplexity, with gains most pronounced on Llama 3 . At a 0.7 compression ratio, KFAC-SVD improves perplexity on WikiText2 by 49 % over the best baseline ( DOBI-SVD ), extending to 66 % with LEMS . Zero-shot accuracy largely follows this trend: under mild compression (0.9), KFAC-SVD avoids the sharp accuracy drop seen in several baselines and stays in the mid- 50 s, while LEMS recovers near-lossless performance ( 61.8 % vs. 63.3 % original). Strictly comparing to prior Fisher-based methods, KFAC-SVD outperforms the baselines by up to 10.3 p.p. without the addition of LEMS . GFWSVD degrades significantly under identical conditions, reaffirming its conditioning challenges. The only exception is Mistral at 0.9, where ASVD achieves a slightly higher zero-shot accuracy (+0.35 p.p. ) despite worse perplexity. This implies Mistral relies on features well-aligned with activation magnitude, favoring simpler proxies in uniform settings. Overall, KFAC-SVD provides the most effective decomposition, especially when compared with other Fisher-based methods, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in the vast majority of evaluated settings.

To assess the scalability of LEMS , we evaluate the Qwen3 family (4B-32B) across five compression ratios (0.5-0.9). To demonstrate that LEMS is agnostic to a particular decomposition objective, we report results for both KFAC-SVD and the activation-based SVD-LLM . Figure 2 contrasts uniform allocation (solid) to LEMS (dashed), with numerical results provided in Supplement D .

Across all budgets and model sizes, LEMS consistently improves both perplexity and downstream utility. Averaged over ratios and models, it reduces perplexity by 17% for KFAC-SVD and 34% for SVD-LLM , while increasing zero-shot accuracy by +7.2 and +9.1 p.p. , respectively. Gains are largest under aggressive compression: at 0.5, LEMS cuts perplexity by ∼ \sim 26% ( KFAC-SVD ) / ∼ \sim 57% ( SVD-LLM ) on average and recovers +4.8 / +8.7 p.p. accuracy. Crucially, it also resolves the sharp accuracy dips observed in Qwen3 -32B under uniform allocation for both decompositions. The benefits extend beyond Qwen3 : on the substantially larger Llama 3 .1-70B, LEMS reduces WikiText2 perplexity from 7.9 to 4.5 and increases accuracy from 62.6 to 66.6 (see Supplement B.6 ). Comparing decompositions methods, KFAC-SVD achieves approximately 26% lower perplexity than SVD-LLM under uniform allocation, demonstrating stronger alignment with the downstream loss. When combined with LEMS , perplexities become tightly matched between the two methods, with SVD-LLM retaining a marginal edge in zero-shot accuracy ( ∼ \sim 0.3 p.p. ). Notably, the larger gains observed for SVD-LLM with LEMS suggest that suboptimal rank allocation is often a primary source of degradation under uniform compression. Differently, through the calibrated layer-wise error model and global ILP optimization, LEMS overcomes the degradation of uniform compression yielding consistent gains.

In the head-to-head comparison without search, due to the differences between standard SVD and BasisSharing , we compare KFAC-SVD against BasisSharing under both matched memory and matched compute budgets using the same data and precision. The results of the comparison are presented in Table 15 . As can be seen, for both matching memory and matching compute our method comes out ahead in perplexity and zero-shot comparisons, positioning it as a capable alternative to BasisSharing in both scenarios.

inspect:2610.26836.question: How were in-context reports and section-index retrieval compared on the same PHREEQC tasks? What controls isolate evidence retrieval from simulation correctness, and what limitations affect transfer to a research-paper digest agent?

passages.text: Each agent has four tools — write_file , read_file (optionally with a line range), list_file , and execute_phreeqc — and works in an isolated workspace for at most 24 steps, committing to an answer by writing it to a file. PHREEQC writes a formatted report ( result.out ) that prints each quantity at the precision the answer options use; agents may also add SELECTED_OUTPUT or USER_PUNCH blocks, which write chosen quantities to separate files with more digits. The conditions differ in what execute_phreeqc returns and in the system-prompt line that describes it (Table 1 ; Appendix B ). We refer to the first as inline and to TOC and Grep as retrieval . Condition What execute_phreeqc returns Inline The report, head/tail-truncated to 100,000 characters TOC Metadata and an index of report sections with starting lines; the agent reads line ranges Grep Metadata only; the agent searches the report with regular expressions Hybrid The report when it fits within 100,000 characters, the TOC otherwise TOC+Report TOC, with an instruction to answer from the report (Section 5 ) TOC+Round TOC, with an instruction to round to the options’ precision (Section 5 ) Table 1: The six ways in which the simulator’s report is delivered. The simulation, the tools, and the step budget are the same in all of them.

We evaluate Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash Preview through their APIs: the Claude models at temperature 0 without extended thinking, the GPT and Gemini models at API defaults with no reasoning-effort setting. Without the simulator, no model exceeds 46.2% with direct or chain-of-thought prompting (the majority-label rate is 32.9%), so the items require the tool (Appendix B , Table 8 ). Gemini 3 Flash gives no parseable answer on 46% of items even inline, so we report it in Appendix G and leave it out of the analyses below.

passages.section: Under retrieval, agents substitute their own output for the report.
passages.text: Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in more than half of their trajectories: no part of it reaches them. In most trajectories they read their own selected-output files (Table 2 , Skip and Own; Figure 1 a). They define such files about as often inline (Table 12 , Def.), but there the report is already in context and they answer from it. We call this evidence substitution : leaving the tool’s canonical report unopened and answering from output that the agent defined itself. Sonnet skips the report in about one of ten TOC trajectories. Figure 3 shows one trajectory of this kind in full: the agent defines a selected-output file in its first input, reads that file after the run, and answers with the truncation of the value it prints, although the index it received points to the section of the report that prints the keyed value. Step Agent call → \rightarrow tool result (abridged) 1 write_file(calc.inp) : SOLUTION 1 Pure water / pH 7 charge / REACTION 1 / H2SO4 1 / 0.001 / SELECTED_OUTPUT -file sel.out -pH true -solution true / END 2 execute_phreeqc(calc.inp) → \rightarrow ok; output_files: phreeqc.log, result.out (6,957 bytes), sel.out (315 bytes); result_out_toc: 19 entries, among them {line 92: Reaction step 1}, {line 112: Solution composition}, {line 118: Description of solution}; hint: Use read_file with start_line/end_line to read specific sections. 3 read_file(sel.out, 1, 200) → \rightarrow sim state soln … step pH pe / 1 i_soln 1 … 6.99738 4 / 1 react 1 … 1 2.75065 14.6924 4 write_file(final_answer.txt) : <<< A >>> – Not read: result.out , line 120 (in “Description of solution” of reaction step 1): pH = 2.751

passages.text: Figure 3: A GPT-5.1 TOC trajectory on item 121 (pH after the first reaction step; options A 2.750, B 2.751, C 2.748, D 2.745; key B), with tool results abridged and “/” marking line breaks. The agent answers A, the truncation of the 2.75065 in its own selected-output file, and never reads the report, which prints the keyed 2.751.

passages.section: Retrieval adds a choice of evidence.
passages.text: The two deliveries make the same report obtainable: every number in the inline report is one read away, and for GPT-5.2, with the simulation held fixed, the loss remains on reports that fit inline. What differs is which output the agent answers from. In our setting, retrieval turns reading the report into a choice of evidence. Inline, one source is in view; under retrieval, the report competes with the files the agent wrote itself, and models that choose badly lose accuracy. The instruction works because it makes that choice for them.

Gemini 3 Flash gives no parseable answer on 46% of items even inline, so we report it in Appendix G and leave it out of the analyses below.

Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in more than half of their trajectories: no part of it reaches them. In most trajectories they read their own selected-output files (Table 2 , Skip and Own; Figure 1 a). They define such files about as often inline (Table 12 , Def.), but there the report is already in context and they answer from it. We call this evidence substitution : leaving the tool’s canonical report unopened and answering from output that the agent defined itself. Sonnet skips the report in about one of ten TOC trajectories. inspect:2610.33846.question: For the CIFAR-10 label-noise experiments, what fraction and type of labels are randomized, which model depths and fixed-feature baselines are compared, and how does test error change after the models fit the noisy labels? How closely do these experiments support the kernel-gradient-flow phase diagram?

passages.text: Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

Figure 1: Generalization along the path to memorization. Test error on 2000 cats and dogs ( x x -axes) versus classification error on the randomly labelled automobiles ( y y -axes) taken from the CIFAR10 dataset. The fixed training set has n = 7000 n=7000 images: 2800 2800 cats, 2800 2800 dogs with their respective labels, and 1400 1400 automobiles with independent random labels. Panels vary the overparametrization ratio κ = P / n ≈ 1 , 10 , 100 \kappa=P/n\approx 1,10,100 , where P P counts optimized parameters. Curves average about 30 completed seeds; a centered arithmetic average of up to seven neighboring recorded times is applied to both coordinates for display, preserving the initial and final values. These parametric curves trace the two errors as training time t t increases. Triangles mark initialization, squares the last iterate and crosses the minimum displayed test error. All trainable networks use square loss and constant-rate Nesterov SGD, without augmentation or weight decay, through 1500 epochs; RF-CNN uses full-batch readout GD through 10 12 10^{12} steps. In Appendix F we provide all numerical details and the unsmoothed trajectories, including training loss.

This question is related to, but distinct from, grokking and benign overfitting. Canonical grokking concerns noiseless, realizable tasks, where training accuracy becomes essentially perfect long before test performance improves ( Power et al., 2022 ) . Here, instead, a considerable fraction of the labels is intrinsically unpredictable, and we ask whether fitting them eventually harms generalization. Benign overfitting asks whether an interpolating estimator can generalize well despite label noise ( Bartlett et al., 2020 ; Liang and Rakhlin, 2020 ) ; it does not by itself determine whether interpolation is optimal relative to earlier points along the training trajectory. Our focus is precisely on this dynamical comparison between early stopping and convergence. Can the minimum test error nevertheless genuinely occur at convergence? Existing theoretical analyses that follow feature-learning dynamics under label noise toward interpolation reach the opposite conclusion for the shallow neural networks they study in the regimes analyzed: fitting the noisy labels eventually degrades generalization, making early stopping preferable ( Han et al., 2025 ; Montanari and Urbani, 2025 ) . They therefore do not account for the empirical hypothesis formulated here. We show that such behavior is possible for square-loss kernel gradient flow in the Rules-and-Facts (RAF) model introduced by Farné et al. (2026) .

We derive exact learning curves and obtain a phase diagram with three regimes, corresponding to three families of kernels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. Thus, even in the presence of extensive label noise, interpolation can lead to a better test error than any early stopping. The kernel analysis therefore produces the behavior that motivated this work. At the critical geometry, the best test error is attained at interpolation, and the corresponding trajectory in Figure 4 closely resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 , whose best test performance is attained after all randomly labelled examples have been classified correctly. The theory thus provides a concrete realization of the observed phenomenon. It does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. Determining which aspects of feature learning, model size, and architecture produce this behavior remains an open question.

In this work, we asked whether the presence of extensive label noise necessarily makes early stopping preferable to interpolation. The noisy CIFAR10 experiments in Fig. 1 and Appendix F support the hypothesis that deep and highly overparameterized neural networks actually do not benefit from early stopping. Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration. Appendix F shows that this observation is robust beyond the setting of Fig. 1 : it persists across a range of training recipes, including cross-entropy, data augmentation, and a scheduled learning rate, as well as across additional optimization controls. We then asked whether the absence of a benefit from early stopping can be reproduced in an analytically solvable setting. Our analysis of high-dimensional learning curves for kernel gradient flow shows that it can. Kernel geometry determines whether the lowest test error occurs at a finite time or at convergence. We identify a critical kernel geometry for which the interpolating predictor attains the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, fitting unpredictable labels need not come at the expense of generalization, in a sense yet considerably stronger than the one known from the literature on benign overfitting.

The critical-kernel trajectory provides a concrete fixed-representation counterpart of the behavior observed in the deeper neural networks: fitting the unpredictable labels does not produce a late-time deterioration of generalization, and the best test error is attained at the end of the trajectory. Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior. The theory nevertheless places the empirical hypothesis formulated in the introduction on a precise footing: even under extensive label noise, the absence of a benefit from early stopping is possible and can be controlled by representation geometry. Understanding how larger and deeper feature-learning architectures realize analogous behavior remains an open question. All the results can be reproduced using the code provided in the repository: https://github.com/SPOC-group/Early-stopping .

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) is now widely accepted as the standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its parameter efficiency arises from a low-rank factorization that is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model where parameter dimension alone cannot describe learning complexity. Singular learning theory overcomes the unsuitability of parameter dimension for capturing learning complexity by instead studying the real log canonical threshold (RLCT)—a geometric quantity which controls the leading asymptotic behavior of Bayesian generalization and model evidence. We study the RLCT for LoRA and, in particular, how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network in which the adaptation is performed. Under a local linearization of the pretrained network, we show that LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback–Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance. This covariance is constructed from the input activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer and determines which low-rank perturbations of the pretrained model are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression. When its kernel meets these directions, however, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters arise and the singular geometry of the model changes. We characterize this geometry both locally, using a decomposition into observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally, using affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. In particular, the global learning complexity is not necessarily determined by the

tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally, using affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. In particular, the global learning complexity is not necessarily determined by the geometry at a ground-truth parameter; it turns out that singularities on a different rank stratum can dominate the asymptotic behavior. To support the numerical study of this geometry, we introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT that accounts for finite-sample variation across inverse temperatures. Numerical experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.
Low-rank adaptation; singular learning theory; real log canonical threshold; low-rank matrix factorization; determinantal varieties.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) has become the standard method for fine-tuning large neural networks due to its parameter efficiency. Instead of updating pre-trained weight matrix W pre ∈ ℝ m × d W_{\text{pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} directly, LoRA freezes W pre W_{\text{pre}} and learns the following low-rank perturbation: W = W pre + B ​ A , B ∈ ℝ m × r , A ∈ ℝ r × d . W=W_{\text{pre}}+BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\,A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}. When r ≪ min ⁡ { m , d } r\ll\min\{m,d\} , the number of trainable parameters reduces significantly, however, a fundamental problem of identifiability also arises, since many pairs of matrices A , B A,B are able to represent the same update B ​ A BA . Approaching the problem of non-identifiability from a geometric perspective is useful in the sense that model parameters representing the same distribution may form a smooth manifold of constant dimension, so then the redundant directions can be removed locally. LoRA, however, turns out to be a singular statistical model. It turns out that the geometry of the factorized parameterization of LoRA changes with the rank of B ​ A BA , which results in a stratified parameter space in which different rank strata meet along singular loci.

Singular learning theory (SLT, Watanabe (2009) ; Watanabe (2018) ) is a methodology adapted for such statistical models where complex local geometry affects the asymptotic learning behavior. In regular models, local asymptotic behavior is controlled by a nondegenerate quadratic approximation to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and model complexity is captured simply by parameter dimension. In singular models, this quadratic approximation breaks down because the set of parameters representing the same distribution may have positive dimension, intersect itself, or change dimension across different strata. The asymptotics are then controlled by the local geometry of the zero set of the KL divergence and not just by the number of identifiable parameters. SLT studies this geometry and measures it using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT), which replaces half the parameter dimension in the leading asymptotics of Bayesian generalization and marginal likelihood. Computing the RLCT is therefore fundamentally a geometric problem that is closely connected to the study of singular algebraic and analytic varieties.

Our work lies at the intersection of theoretical analyses of low-rank adaptation and singular learning theory. We now review existing literature and theory on LoRA and the local-linearization perspective on fine-tuning, as well as related work on surgical fine-tuning and choice of layers to adapt. We then position our work within the literature on RLCTs of singular statistical models and recent applications of SLT to neural networks. Finally, since our empirical analysis requires numerical computation of the RLCT, we review existing approaches to RLCT estimation and their relation to the estimator introduced in this work.

inspect:2610.31728.question: In the LLM pretraining study, what models, token budgets, optimizer baselines, learning-rate controls, and measured loss or throughput results support Muon's proposed structured-gradient-noise mechanism? Which results are only from associative-memory models?

passages.text: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon’s preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast–slow momentum. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

Muon has emerged as a prominent alternative to Adam for training the matrix parameters of large language models (LLMs) ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its defining operation replaces a gradient or momentum matrix by an approximate polar factor, flattening its nonzero singular values before the parameter update. This matrix-level normalization offers a different way to allocate updates across directions from Adam’s coordinatewise rescaling. Recent frontier-model reports, including DeepSeek–V4.1–Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) and Kimi–K3 ( Kimi Team and others, 2026 ) , adopt Muon variants for matrix optimization, with head-wise orthogonalization further adapting the update to attention structure. These developments make understanding when and why Muon improves learning an increasingly practical theoretical question.

Existing theory has established convergence guarantees for practical orthogonalization procedures ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ) and identified preconditioning benefits in structured optimization problems ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Full-batch associative-memory analyses further show how spectral normalization can balance learning across tasks with heterogeneous frequencies ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . In LLM pretraining, however, Muon acts on stochastic mini-batch gradients, and nonlinear normalization need not preserve the benefits predicted from population gradients. In particular, writing msgn \operatorname{msgn} for the partial polar map, generally 𝔼 ⁡ [ msgn ⁡ ( G t ) ∣ W t ] ≠ msgn ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ G t ∣ W t ] ) \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{msgn}(G_{t})\mid W_{t}]\neq\operatorname{msgn}(\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mid W_{t}]) . Recent work has begun to characterize stochastic spectral dynamics and geometry-dependent noise scales ( Paquette et al., 2026 ; Naganuma et al., 2026 ) ; the interaction between task occurrence, gradient reliability, and temporal averaging motivates the question we study here: Q1: When does Muon retain a directional learning advantage under stochastic gradient noise, and how do noise structure, batch size, and momentum determine this advantage?

Isotropic noise limits preconditioning. Standard stochastic optimization analyses often control gradient noise through a scalar variance bound ( Ghadimi and Lan, 2013 ) , leaving its directional structure unspecified. We use isotropic Gaussian noise as a diagnostic baseline. In the fixed-dimensional low-SNR limit, we prove that Muon’s conditional mean update is, to first order, a scalar multiple of the population gradient, as confirmed numerically in Figure 1 . SGD with a matched learning rate therefore reproduces this first-order mean drift: applying the partial polar map to each stochastic mini-batch gradient does not, by itself, produce directional preconditioning in the first-order mean response. Explaining such gains in this regime requires examining noise structure. Sampling controls balancing. We study associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies p j p_{j} ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Mini-batch sampling can leave task directions entirely unobserved; without momentum, Muon’s nullspace preservation then prevents updates along those directions. inspect:2610.30676.question: Across the five Llama and Qwen models, how do post-hoc singular-value smoothing and spiking of up_proj and down_proj affect measured task quality? What unperturbed and random-perturbation controls, intervention strengths, and uncertainty estimates support a causal interpretation?

passages.text: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches these deviations, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller relative to the geometric mean (spiking); and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness/hallucination/safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

(a) Schematic illustration of the singular-value perturbation applied to feed-forward projection matrices. (b) Trait-level response profiles under spectral perturbation, showing how behavior shifts across models and perturbation strengths. (c) Selected task-level outcomes, highlighting that the same perturbation can improve some subtasks while degrading others. Figure 1: Overview of the perturbation setup and representative behavioral effects. Panel (a) visualizes the SVD-based perturbation schema, panel (b) summarizes trait-level responses, and panel (c) highlights selective task-level changes induced by the intervention. Large language model behavior is usually analyzed through prompting, finetuning, or activation-level interventions. By contrast, we ask whether a small, interpretable change to pretrained weight spectra is already enough to expose structure in downstream behavior. The singular values of transformer MLP projections summarize how strongly each layer amplifies different directions; if that spectral geometry carries functional information, then changing it in a controlled way should produce at least partly systematic behavioral effects rather than only unstructured noise. We therefore study a constrained intervention on feed-forward projections in which singular values are reweighted around their geometric mean while the corresponding singular vectors are left unchanged. This makes spectral inequality itself the manipulated variable and lets us ask whether broad capability patterns can be reorganized without changing tokenization, prompts, or optimization. Figure 1 previews the three complementary views used throughout the paper: the intervention itself, broad behavioral shifts, and concrete task-level gains and losses.

The empirical picture that emerges is not one of uniform quality loss. Instead, spectral smoothing and spiking redistribute behavior across benchmark modules, auxiliary tasks, and personality-style probes. Some settings mainly suppress language and deductive responses, while others preserve or even improve specific factual or task-local behaviors. The goal of the paper is therefore not to identify a universally best α \alpha , but to characterize which capabilities become more or less available under controlled spectral perturbation. Our main contributions are threefold: • We introduce a lightweight singular-value smoothing/spiking intervention for transformer MLP projections and evaluate it across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . • We build a subtask-level capability-response analysis over 118 subtasks, using a retained three-dimensional basis of Factual Knowledge , Language Understanding , and Deductive Reasoning . • We provide evidence that spectral perturbations induce non-uniform tradeoffs across capability-labeled benchmark modules, auxiliary tasks, judge-scored truthfulness/hallucination/safety evaluations, and TRAIT personality probes ( Lee et al., 2024 ) , and we relate this heterogeneity to non-uniform layerwise spectral sensitivity.

Even with those limits, the intervention is attractive because it is post-hoc, architecture-aware, and easy to audit. The results motivate future variants such as layer-normalized α \alpha , projection-specific controls for up_proj and down_proj , or expert-wise safeguards for MoE models. More broadly, they suggest that weight-space spectral statistics are a useful handle for probing how different capabilities are bundled together in large language models.

The Gini plot shows that spectral inequality differs substantially by layer, model, and projection. Dense Llama models exhibit strong depth dependence, especially in up_proj ; Qwen3 8B has unusually concentrated early layers; and Qwen3 30B-A3B MoE adds expert-level variation, where the maximum expert can deviate substantially from the layer mean. The relative top-singular-value plot identifies where the same global perturbation causes the largest multiplicative amplification or suppression, with the strongest effects occurring in layers whose top singular value is already far above the geometric mean. Model / proj. Layer Base Gini Top-SV multiplier Qwen3 8B / down_proj 1 0.3209 1.7984 Qwen3 8B / down_proj 2 0.3513 1.7278 Llama 3.2 3B Instruct / up_proj 27 0.2506 1.6784 Llama 3.1 8B Instruct / up_proj 31 0.2143 1.6535 Qwen3 8B / up_proj 2 0.3910 1.6443 Table 9: Examples of large top-singular-value amplification at α = + 0.2 \alpha=+0.2 . These cases illustrate that the same global perturbation can produce markedly different realized updates across layers.

Using one global α \alpha remains useful as a controlled intervention, but it should be interpreted as a spectrum-dependent perturbation rather than a uniform update. This explains why α \alpha sweeps can produce selective task improvements or degradations rather than smooth global quality changes. The layer-wise diagnostics motivate safer future variants such as layer-normalized α \alpha , projection-specific α \alpha for up_proj and down_proj , MoE expert clipping, and reporting realized spectral statistics alongside the nominal α \alpha value.

selections.summary: The paper attributes instability at large asymmetric LoRA learning-rate ratios to initialization-induced noise and proposes a smaller-variance initialization. It reports a wider stable learning-rate region across ranks and update multipliers.
selections.relevance: Directly informs LoRA optimization and hyperparameter selection in practical language-model fine-tuning.

The LLM experiments cover both encoder-only models (RoBERTa-base on GLUE) and decoder-only models (Llama arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks, with additional backbones in the appendix).

selections.summary: On matrix quadratics, the paper analyzes when Muon's polar update helps or slows optimization. It argues that a finite number of Newton–Schulz steps can handle tiny singular modes better than exact orthogonalization, then measures such modes in a Muon-trained transformer.

selections.summary: In a noisy CIFAR-10 task, larger, deeper networks attain their best observed test performance after fitting the randomly labeled examples, unlike fixed-feature and shallower models. A separate kernel-gradient-flow analysis gives a phase diagram for when early stopping helps.

Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior.

selections.summary: A controlled agent study compares receiving a scientific tool's report inline with retrieving it through an index. Some models lose accuracy under retrieval because they answer from self-created output rather than the canonical report.
selections.relevance: Offers a concrete failure mode for a handwritten research-digest harness that retrieves passages and requires source-grounded answers.

evidence.quote: The simulation, the tools, and the step budget are the same in all of them.
Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in more than half of their trajectories: no part of it reaches them.

selections.summary: The paper applies post-hoc singular-value smoothing and spiking to transformer feed-forward projections in five Llama and Qwen instruction models. It reports non-uniform changes across evaluated tasks, with sensitivity varying by model and layerwise spectrum.

The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality.

matches.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. 2610.31897:a5b4387804b54cd2bf80279a69eaa.question: Which language-model architectures and sizes are evaluated, and how do S-SALAAD's quality, compression ratio, and inference speed compare with dense, low-rank-only, and sparse-plus-low-rank baselines under matched budgets?

passages.text: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

The L L -only variant is the S ≡ 0 S\equiv 0 special case of S-SALAAD. It retains ADMM’s coupled updates of X X and L L under the constraint X = L X\!=\!L , with the proximal update ( 8 ) explicitly removing small singular values from L L . This structure-learning procedure goes beyond directly adding a low-rank regularizer to the task loss. Figure 8 compares this variant with direct subgradient optimization of ℓ ⁡ ( X ) + λ ​ | X | ∗ \ell(X)\!+\!\lambda|X|_{*} . With λ = 10 − 6 \lambda\!=\!10^{-6} , perplexity is comparable to that of L L -only S-SALAAD at the largest budget but rises sharply as the budget decreases. This behavior is consistent with low-rank structure that is too weak to support aggressive compression. Increasing λ \lambda to 10 − 5 10^{-5} strengthens rank regularization and yields nearly constant perplexity across the tested budgets, supporting elastic compression at the cost of higher perplexity throughout. Except for the separately sourced LORO reference described below, perplexity is measured on held-out tokens of the training corpus—C4 for Llama and FineWeb-Edu for Qwen3-1.7B—under the corresponding evaluation protocol. Perplexities are compared within each model family, not across the two corpora. We evaluate zero-shot downstream accuracy on ARC-Easy, OpenBookQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, and SciQ using the LM Evaluation Harness ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . Baseline implementations and profiling. Vanilla training and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) provide training references, while the L L -only special case ( S ≡ 0 S\equiv 0 ) provides a reference for block granularity. EGAR produces variants at multiple parameter budgets from each S-SALAAD checkpoint without calibration data. All compressed models are evaluated without additional fine-tuning for fair comparison. 2610.30280:a7e8eec0ac1f3c7c9a1097b568f63.question: What transformer or language-model training experiments compare Muon or PolarGD with AdamW or gradient descent, and what measured performance differences and experimental controls support the claimed benefit of Newton–Schulz iterations?

passages.text: Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

Muon updates matrix-valued parameters along approximately orthogonalized directions and often trains large language models faster than AdamW , yet it remains unclear when and why orthogonalization helps. We study PolarGD , the orthogonalized update at the core of Muon , on matrix quadratics, where optimizers can be analyzed in closed form, and compare update directions under line search to remove the effect of learning-rate tuning. Orthogonalization pays off when the gradient is far from low rank and its largest singular directions see high curvature. PolarGD reaches the minimizer in one step whenever the rows of the error are orthogonal with equal norms, for any Hessian, whereas gradient descent needs all Hessian eigenvalues to be equal; and unlike sign descent, PolarGD is unaffected by rotations of the problem. Over many steps, PolarGD acts as gradient descent preconditioned by the current iterate, so its speed is governed by the conditioning of the iterate rather than of the Hessian. This explains fast regimes as well as a slow one, caused by tiny singular values of the iterate, in which PolarGD is much slower than gradient descent. Finally, the few Newton--Schulz iterations used in Muon treat these tiny singular values as gradient descent does, so fewer iterations can converge faster than exact orthogonalization; in a transformer trained with Muon , about a quarter of the singular values of the attention matrices fall in this regime.

2610.32142:6e6bc08b3b51ede029ec7709d5d9d.question: In practical LLM fine-tuning, which models, tasks, and baselines are used to compare the proposed initialization with standard LoRA initialization and LoRA+? How do performance and training stability vary across asymmetric learning-rate ratios, with matched tuning and adapter ranks?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix B B than for the down-projection matrix A A . However, the ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal–noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard Init[A] , the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for B B , η B \eta_{B} , the initialization scale β \beta , and the adapter rank r r . In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple initialization that scales the variance of A A as σ A 2 ∝ n − 2 \sigma_{A}^{2}\propto n^{-2} while keeping B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1 / n 1/n , stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Across tasks and models, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard Init[A] , and makes the width-based guideline η B ≈ n ​ η A \eta_{B}\approx n\eta_{A} a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 22 ] is a standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) [ 21 , 35 , 33 ] . Given a width- n n LoRA layer with pretrained weight W ∈ ℝ n × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and input Z ¯ ∈ ℝ n \underline{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , LoRA uses Z ¯ = W ​ Z ¯ + α r ​ B ​ A ​ Z ¯ \bar{Z}=W\underline{Z}+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\underline{Z} , where A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable with learning rates (LRs) η A \eta_{A} and η B \eta_{B} . Here r ≪ n r\ll n is the adapter rank and α / r \alpha/r is the LoRA update multiplier. We use β \beta to denote the initialization-magnitude hyperparameter: standard LoRA initialization, denoted Init[A] , initializes B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and initializes A 0 A_{0} randomly with mean zero and standard deviation β n − 1 / 2 \beta n^{-1/2} , so the adapter preserves the pretrained model output at step zero. Figure 1 : Overview of LoRA initialization and feature-norm stability. Left : LoRA branch notation and the initialization scalings compared in this work, including standard Init[A] , Init[AB] , and the proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] . Right : feature-norm trajectories at width n = 4096 n=4096 for different initialization scales β \beta . Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] keeps the LoRA features nearly invariant to β \beta , while the alternative scalings exhibit stronger initialization-dependent growth.

Despite its simplicity, LoRA is sensitive to hyperparameters (HPs). The rank r r controls the expressive capacity of the adapter [ 60 ] , but its effect is inseparable from the update multiplier λ r = α / r \lambda_{r}=\alpha/r . Kalajdzievski [ 27 ] shows that the conventional choice α / r \alpha/r is not rank-stabilized: it can shrink adapter activations and gradients as r r grows, slowing learning at high ranks and motivating the alternative α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} . LRs introduce a further source of brittleness. Recent empirical work shows that, after sufficiently broad LR sweeps, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants [ 32 ] . This shifts the practical question from only designing new adapters to understanding LoRA HP selection. LoRA+ [ 17 ] gives a principled route toward understanding LR selection by assigning different LRs to the two LoRA matrices. Its infinite-width feature learning analysis suggests that efficient LoRA feature updates require an asymmetric regime with η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} and, under idealized scaling assumptions, a ratio η B / η A ≈ n \eta_{B}/\eta_{A}\approx n . We write this ratio as ρ = η B / η A \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A} . The asymmetric regime is attractive because B B directly controls the LoRA branch output, so increasing η B \eta_{B} can accelerate adaptation. In finite pretrained LLMs, however, ρ \rho often becomes another hyperparameter to tune: large ratios can improve performance, but under Init[A] they can also trigger instability. We address the gap between the theoretical LR guidance and practical LLM fine-tuning in this paper.

We show that the fragility of asymmetric LRs comes from an initialization-dependent noise term that survives even though the LoRA branch has zero output at initialization. Although B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , the random matrix A 0 A_{0} affects the branch as soon as B B moves away from zero. A signal–noise decomposition of the LoRA feature update reveals two components: a task-driven signal from optimizer updates and a noise term from the interaction between the learned B B and the random initial A A . Both terms scale with η B \eta_{B} , so increasing η B \eta_{B} amplifies useful adaptation and initialization noise at the same time. In the small-LR regime common in pretrained LLM fine-tuning, the signal can remain controlled while the Init[A] noise contribution does not vanish with width, making large ρ \rho , large initialization scale β \beta , and large update multiplier α / r \alpha/r especially brittle.

We evaluate whether Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] improves HP transfer and robustness in two settings: a controlled toy MLP and LLM fine-tuning. The LLM experiments cover both encoder-only models (RoBERTa-base on GLUE) and decoder-only models (Llama arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks, with additional backbones in the appendix). Across experiments, we vary the initialization scale β \beta , LR ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} , adapter rank r r , and LoRA multiplier α / r \alpha/r ; Init[A] uses base variance σ A 2 = 1 / n \sigma_{A}^{2}=1/n and Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] uses σ A 2 = 1 / n 2 \sigma_{A}^{2}=1/n^{2} , both with B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Full training details are in Appendix C .

2610.32878:9ac3aa6123aa1ab27599138cf12e4.question: At matched parameter or compression budgets, which SVD-based LLM compression baselines are compared with LEMS and KFAC-SVD on Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3? What are the measured perplexity and zero-shot accuracy differences, and how are calibration data, recovery fine-tuning, and model sizes controlled?

passages.text: We evaluate KFAC-SVD against state-of-the-art methods across three LLM families: Mistral , Llama 3 , and Qwen3 . Table 2 details the results for all approaches under uniform compression rates (0.9, 0.7) and calibration sample count, with an additional line for our search-enhanced variant. KFAC-SVD consistently yields the lowest perplexity, with gains most pronounced on Llama 3 . At a 0.7 compression ratio, KFAC-SVD improves perplexity on WikiText2 by 49 % over the best baseline ( DOBI-SVD ), extending to 66 % with LEMS . Zero-shot accuracy largely follows this trend: under mild compression (0.9), KFAC-SVD avoids the sharp accuracy drop seen in several baselines and stays in the mid- 50 s, while LEMS recovers near-lossless performance ( 61.8 % vs. 63.3 % original). Strictly comparing to prior Fisher-based methods, KFAC-SVD outperforms the baselines by up to 10.3 p.p. without the addition of LEMS . GFWSVD degrades significantly under identical conditions, reaffirming its conditioning challenges. The only exception is Mistral at 0.9, where ASVD achieves a slightly higher zero-shot accuracy (+0.35 p.p. ) despite worse perplexity. This implies Mistral relies on features well-aligned with activation magnitude, favoring simpler proxies in uniform settings. Overall, KFAC-SVD provides the most effective decomposition, especially when compared with other Fisher-based methods, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in the vast majority of evaluated settings.

To assess the scalability of LEMS , we evaluate the Qwen3 family (4B-32B) across five compression ratios (0.5-0.9). To demonstrate that LEMS is agnostic to a particular decomposition objective, we report results for both KFAC-SVD and the activation-based SVD-LLM . Figure 2 contrasts uniform allocation (solid) to LEMS (dashed), with numerical results provided in Supplement D .

Across all budgets and model sizes, LEMS consistently improves both perplexity and downstream utility. Averaged over ratios and models, it reduces perplexity by 17% for KFAC-SVD and 34% for SVD-LLM , while increasing zero-shot accuracy by +7.2 and +9.1 p.p. , respectively. Gains are largest under aggressive compression: at 0.5, LEMS cuts perplexity by ∼ \sim 26% ( KFAC-SVD ) / ∼ \sim 57% ( SVD-LLM ) on average and recovers +4.8 / +8.7 p.p. accuracy. Crucially, it also resolves the sharp accuracy dips observed in Qwen3 -32B under uniform allocation for both decompositions. The benefits extend beyond Qwen3 : on the substantially larger Llama 3 .1-70B, LEMS reduces WikiText2 perplexity from 7.9 to 4.5 and increases accuracy from 62.6 to 66.6 (see Supplement B.6 ). Comparing decompositions methods, KFAC-SVD achieves approximately 26% lower perplexity than SVD-LLM under uniform allocation, demonstrating stronger alignment with the downstream loss. When combined with LEMS , perplexities become tightly matched between the two methods, with SVD-LLM retaining a marginal edge in zero-shot accuracy ( ∼ \sim 0.3 p.p. ). Notably, the larger gains observed for SVD-LLM with LEMS suggest that suboptimal rank allocation is often a primary source of degradation under uniform compression. Differently, through the calibrated layer-wise error model and global ILP optimization, LEMS overcomes the degradation of uniform compression yielding consistent gains.

As can be seen, for both matching memory and matching compute our method comes out ahead in perplexity and zero-shot comparisons, positioning it as a capable alternative to BasisSharing in both scenarios.

2610.26836:c73b5f69c3a5fede16d4f7c124c20.question: How were in-context reports and section-index retrieval compared on the same PHREEQC tasks? What controls isolate evidence retrieval from simulation correctness, and what limitations affect transfer to a research-paper digest agent?

passages.text: Each agent has four tools — write_file , read_file (optionally with a line range), list_file , and execute_phreeqc — and works in an isolated workspace for at most 24 steps, committing to an answer by writing it to a file. PHREEQC writes a formatted report ( result.out ) that prints each quantity at the precision the answer options use; agents may also add SELECTED_OUTPUT or USER_PUNCH blocks, which write chosen quantities to separate files with more digits. The conditions differ in what execute_phreeqc returns and in the system-prompt line that describes it (Table 1 ; Appendix B ). We refer to the first as inline and to TOC and Grep as retrieval . The simulation, the tools, and the step budget are the same in all of them.

We evaluate Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash Preview through their APIs: the Claude models at temperature 0 without extended thinking, the GPT and Gemini models at API defaults with no reasoning-effort setting. Without the simulator, no model exceeds 46.2% with direct or chain-of-thought prompting (the majority-label rate is 32.9%), so the items require the tool (Appendix B , Table 8 ). Gemini 3 Flash gives no parseable answer on 46% of items even inline, so we report it in Appendix G and leave it out of the analyses below.

passages.section: Under retrieval, agents substitute their own output for the report.
passages.text: Under TOC, GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 skip the report in more than half of their trajectories: no part of it reaches them. In most trajectories they read their own selected-output files (Table 2 , Skip and Own; Figure 1 a). They define such files about as often inline (Table 12 , Def.), but there the report is already in context and they answer from it. We call this evidence substitution : leaving the tool’s canonical report unopened and answering from output that the agent defined itself. Sonnet skips the report in about one of ten TOC trajectories. passages.section: Retrieval adds a choice of evidence.
passages.text: The two deliveries make the same report obtainable: every number in the inline report is one read away, and for GPT-5.2, with the simulation held fixed, the loss remains on reports that fit inline. What differs is which output the agent answers from. In our setting, retrieval turns reading the report into a choice of evidence. Inline, one source is in view; under retrieval, the report competes with the files the agent wrote itself, and models that choose badly lose accuracy. The instruction works because it makes that choice for them.
