2610.33846:3c8512e39e8ddf48624b441927ed0.question: For the CIFAR-10 label-noise experiments, what fraction and type of labels are randomized, which model depths and fixed-feature baselines are compared, and how does test error change after the models fit the noisy labels? How closely do these experiments support the kernel-gradient-flow phase diagram?

passages.text: Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

Figure 1: Generalization along the path to memorization. Test error on 2000 cats and dogs ( x x -axes) versus classification error on the randomly labelled automobiles ( y y -axes) taken from the CIFAR10 dataset. The fixed training set has n = 7000 n=7000 images: 2800 2800 cats, 2800 2800 dogs with their respective labels, and 1400 1400 automobiles with independent random labels. Panels vary the overparametrization ratio κ = P / n ≈ 1 , 10 , 100 \kappa=P/n\approx 1,10,100 , where P P counts optimized parameters. Curves average about 30 completed seeds; a centered arithmetic average of up to seven neighboring recorded times is applied to both coordinates for display, preserving the initial and final values. These parametric curves trace the two errors as training time t t increases. Triangles mark initialization, squares the last iterate and crosses the minimum displayed test error. All trainable networks use square loss and constant-rate Nesterov SGD, without augmentation or weight decay, through 1500 epochs; RF-CNN uses full-batch readout GD through 10 12 10^{12} steps. In Appendix F we provide all numerical details and the unsmoothed trajectories, including training loss.

This question is related to, but distinct from, grokking and benign overfitting. Canonical grokking concerns noiseless, realizable tasks, where training accuracy becomes essentially perfect long before test performance improves ( Power et al., 2022 ) . Here, instead, a considerable fraction of the labels is intrinsically unpredictable, and we ask whether fitting them eventually harms generalization. Benign overfitting asks whether an interpolating estimator can generalize well despite label noise ( Bartlett et al., 2020 ; Liang and Rakhlin, 2020 ) ; it does not by itself determine whether interpolation is optimal relative to earlier points along the training trajectory. Our focus is precisely on this dynamical comparison between early stopping and convergence. Can the minimum test error nevertheless genuinely occur at convergence? Existing theoretical analyses that follow feature-learning dynamics under label noise toward interpolation reach the opposite conclusion for the shallow neural networks they study in the regimes analyzed: fitting the noisy labels eventually degrades generalization, making early stopping preferable ( Han et al., 2025 ; Montanari and Urbani, 2025 ) . They therefore do not account for the empirical hypothesis formulated here. We show that such behavior is possible for square-loss kernel gradient flow in the Rules-and-Facts (RAF) model introduced by Farné et al. (2026) .

We derive exact learning curves and obtain a phase diagram with three regimes, corresponding to three families of kernels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. Thus, even in the presence of extensive label noise, interpolation can lead to a better test error than any early stopping. The kernel analysis therefore produces the behavior that motivated this work. At the critical geometry, the best test error is attained at interpolation, and the corresponding trajectory in Figure 4 closely resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 , whose best test performance is attained after all randomly labelled examples have been classified correctly. The theory thus provides a concrete realization of the observed phenomenon. It does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. Determining which aspects of feature learning, model size, and architecture produce this behavior remains an open question.

In this work, we asked whether the presence of extensive label noise necessarily makes early stopping preferable to interpolation. The noisy CIFAR10 experiments in Fig. 1 and Appendix F support the hypothesis that deep and highly overparameterized neural networks actually do not benefit from early stopping. Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration. Appendix F shows that this observation is robust beyond the setting of Fig. 1 : it persists across a range of training recipes, including cross-entropy, data augmentation, and a scheduled learning rate, as well as across additional optimization controls. We then asked whether the absence of a benefit from early stopping can be reproduced in an analytically solvable setting. Our analysis of high-dimensional learning curves for kernel gradient flow shows that it can. Kernel geometry determines whether the lowest test error occurs at a finite time or at convergence. We identify a critical kernel geometry for which the interpolating predictor attains the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, fitting unpredictable labels need not come at the expense of generalization, in a sense yet considerably stronger than the one known from the literature on benign overfitting.

The critical-kernel trajectory provides a concrete fixed-representation counterpart of the behavior observed in the deeper neural networks: fitting the unpredictable labels does not produce a late-time deterioration of generalization, and the best test error is attained at the end of the trajectory. Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior. The theory nevertheless places the empirical hypothesis formulated in the introduction on a precise footing: even under extensive label noise, the absence of a benefit from early stopping is possible and can be controlled by representation geometry. Understanding how larger and deeper feature-learning architectures realize analogous behavior remains an open question. All the results can be reproduced using the code provided in the repository: https://github.com/SPOC-group/Early-stopping .

2610.32854:0af979bf7fb5df9f236e0e956c42c.question: What assumptions delimit the real log canonical threshold analysis of LoRA, and are there LLM fine-tuning experiments or concrete predictions about adapter rank, optimization, or generalization that validate the theory?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) is now widely accepted as the standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its parameter efficiency arises from a low-rank factorization that is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model where parameter dimension alone cannot describe learning complexity. Singular learning theory overcomes the unsuitability of parameter dimension for capturing learning complexity by instead studying the real log canonical threshold (RLCT)—a geometric quantity which controls the leading asymptotic behavior of Bayesian generalization and model evidence. We study the RLCT for LoRA and, in particular, how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network in which the adaptation is performed. Under a local linearization of the pretrained network, we show that LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback–Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance. This covariance is constructed from the input activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer and determines which low-rank perturbations of the pretrained model are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression. When its kernel meets these directions, however, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters arise and the singular geometry of the model changes. We characterize this geometry both locally, using a decomposition into observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally, using affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. In particular, the global learning complexity is not necessarily determined by the

tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally, using affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. In particular, the global learning complexity is not necessarily determined by the geometry at a ground-truth parameter; it turns out that singularities on a different rank stratum can dominate the asymptotic behavior. To support the numerical study of this geometry, we introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT that accounts for finite-sample variation across inverse temperatures. Numerical experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.
Low-rank adaptation; singular learning theory; real log canonical threshold; low-rank matrix factorization; determinantal varieties.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) has become the standard method for fine-tuning large neural networks due to its parameter efficiency. Instead of updating pre-trained weight matrix W pre ∈ ℝ m × d W_{\text{pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} directly, LoRA freezes W pre W_{\text{pre}} and learns the following low-rank perturbation: W = W pre + B ​ A , B ∈ ℝ m × r , A ∈ ℝ r × d . W=W_{\text{pre}}+BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\,A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}. When r ≪ min ⁡ { m , d } r\ll\min\{m,d\} , the number of trainable parameters reduces significantly, however, a fundamental problem of identifiability also arises, since many pairs of matrices A , B A,B are able to represent the same update B ​ A BA . Approaching the problem of non-identifiability from a geometric perspective is useful in the sense that model parameters representing the same distribution may form a smooth manifold of constant dimension, so then the redundant directions can be removed locally. LoRA, however, turns out to be a singular statistical model. It turns out that the geometry of the factorized parameterization of LoRA changes with the rank of B ​ A BA , which results in a stratified parameter space in which different rank strata meet along singular loci.

Singular learning theory (SLT, Watanabe (2009) ; Watanabe (2018) ) is a methodology adapted for such statistical models where complex local geometry affects the asymptotic learning behavior. In regular models, local asymptotic behavior is controlled by a nondegenerate quadratic approximation to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and model complexity is captured simply by parameter dimension. In singular models, this quadratic approximation breaks down because the set of parameters representing the same distribution may have positive dimension, intersect itself, or change dimension across different strata. The asymptotics are then controlled by the local geometry of the zero set of the KL divergence and not just by the number of identifiable parameters. SLT studies this geometry and measures it using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT), which replaces half the parameter dimension in the leading asymptotics of Bayesian generalization and marginal likelihood. Computing the RLCT is therefore fundamentally a geometric problem that is closely connected to the study of singular algebraic and analytic varieties.

Our work lies at the intersection of theoretical analyses of low-rank adaptation and singular learning theory. We now review existing literature and theory on LoRA and the local-linearization perspective on fine-tuning, as well as related work on surgical fine-tuning and choice of layers to adapt. We then position our work within the literature on RLCTs of singular statistical models and recent applications of SLT to neural networks. Finally, since our empirical analysis requires numerical computation of the RLCT, we review existing approaches to RLCT estimation and their relation to the estimator introduced in this work.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. (2021) ) has become the standard method for fine-tuning large neural networks due to its parameter efficiency. Instead of updating pre-trained weight matrix W pre ∈ ℝ m × d W_{\text{pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} directly, LoRA freezes W pre W_{\text{pre}} and learns the following low-rank perturbation: W = W pre + B ​ A , B ∈ ℝ m × r , A ∈ ℝ r × d . W=W_{\text{pre}}+BA,\qquad B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\,A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}. When r ≪ min ⁡ { m , d } r\ll\min\{m,d\} , the number of trainable parameters reduces significantly, however, a fundamental problem of identifiability also arises, since many pairs of matrices A , B A,B are able to represent the same update B ​ A BA . Approaching the problem of non-identifiability from a geometric perspective is useful in the sense that model parameters representing the same distribution may form a smooth manifold of constant dimension, so then the redundant directions can be removed locally. LoRA, however, turns out to be a singular statistical model. It turns out that the geometry of the factorized parameterization of LoRA changes with the rank of B ​ A BA , which results in a stratified parameter space in which different rank strata meet along singular loci.

Singular learning theory (SLT, Watanabe (2009) ; Watanabe (2018) ) is a methodology adapted for such statistical models where complex local geometry affects the asymptotic learning behavior. In regular models, local asymptotic behavior is controlled by a nondegenerate quadratic approximation to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and model complexity is captured simply by parameter dimension. In singular models, this quadratic approximation breaks down because the set of parameters representing the same distribution may have positive dimension, intersect itself, or change dimension across different strata. The asymptotics are then controlled by the local geometry of the zero set of the KL divergence and not just by the number of identifiable parameters. SLT studies this geometry and measures it using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT), which replaces half the parameter dimension in the leading asymptotics of Bayesian generalization and marginal likelihood. Computing the RLCT is therefore fundamentally a geometric problem that is closely connected to the study of singular algebraic and analytic varieties.

Our work lies at the intersection of theoretical analyses of low-rank adaptation and singular learning theory. We now review existing literature and theory on LoRA and the local-linearization perspective on fine-tuning, as well as related work on surgical fine-tuning and choice of layers to adapt. We then position our work within the literature on RLCTs of singular statistical models and recent applications of SLT to neural networks. Finally, since our empirical analysis requires numerical computation of the RLCT, we review existing approaches to RLCT estimation and their relation to the estimator introduced in this work.

Muon has emerged as a prominent alternative to Adam for training the matrix parameters of large language models (LLMs) ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its defining operation replaces a gradient or momentum matrix by an approximate polar factor, flattening its nonzero singular values before the parameter update. This matrix-level normalization offers a different way to allocate updates across directions from Adam’s coordinatewise rescaling. Recent frontier-model reports, including DeepSeek–V4.1–Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) and Kimi–K3 ( Kimi Team and others, 2026 ) , adopt Muon variants for matrix optimization, with head-wise orthogonalization further adapting the update to attention structure. These developments make understanding when and why Muon improves learning an increasingly practical theoretical question.

Existing theory has established convergence guarantees for practical orthogonalization procedures ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ) and identified preconditioning benefits in structured optimization problems ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Full-batch associative-memory analyses further show how spectral normalization can balance learning across tasks with heterogeneous frequencies ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . In LLM pretraining, however, Muon acts on stochastic mini-batch gradients, and nonlinear normalization need not preserve the benefits predicted from population gradients. In particular, writing msgn \operatorname{msgn} for the partial polar map, generally 𝔼 ⁡ [ msgn ⁡ ( G t ) ∣ W t ] ≠ msgn ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ G t ∣ W t ] ) \mathbb{E}[\operatorname{msgn}(G_{t})\mid W_{t}]\neq\operatorname{msgn}(\mathbb{E}[G_{t}\mid W_{t}]) . Recent work has begun to characterize stochastic spectral dynamics and geometry-dependent noise scales ( Paquette et al., 2026 ; Naganuma et al., 2026 ) ; the interaction between task occurrence, gradient reliability, and temporal averaging motivates the question we study here: Q1: When does Muon retain a directional learning advantage under stochastic gradient noise, and how do noise structure, batch size, and momentum determine this advantage?

Isotropic noise limits preconditioning. Standard stochastic optimization analyses often control gradient noise through a scalar variance bound ( Ghadimi and Lan, 2013 ) , leaving its directional structure unspecified. We use isotropic Gaussian noise as a diagnostic baseline. In the fixed-dimensional low-SNR limit, we prove that Muon’s conditional mean update is, to first order, a scalar multiple of the population gradient, as confirmed numerically in Figure 1 . SGD with a matched learning rate therefore reproduces this first-order mean drift: applying the partial polar map to each stochastic mini-batch gradient does not, by itself, produce directional preconditioning in the first-order mean response. Explaining such gains in this regime requires examining noise structure. Sampling controls balancing. We study associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies p j p_{j} ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Mini-batch sampling can leave task directions entirely unobserved; without momentum, Muon’s nullspace preservation then prevents updates along those directions. For two tasks, we prove an exact balancing threshold B bal B_{\rm bal} : below it, margins grow at unequal linear rates; above it, their gap has uniformly bounded exponential moments. For rare tasks, B bal ∼ ( log ⁡ 2 ) / p min B_{\rm bal}\sim(\log 2)/p_{\min} . In a higher-rank hierarchy, local perturbation estimates identify the expected task count B ​ p j Bp_{j} as a controlling scale. Experiments exhibit corresponding frequency-dependent crossovers, with frequent groups approaching balanced growth while rare groups remain occurrence-limited.

Label noise limits reliability. Label fluctuations persist at the population optimum, so frequent observation alone does not ensure a reliable gradient. Exact gradient statistics and a scalar projected counting model distinguish regimes governed by task counts B ​ p j Bp_{j} and corruption counts B ​ p j ​ ρ α Bp_{j}\rho_{\alpha} . Near the noisy optimum, an isotropic covariance closure with a locally homogeneous frequency approximation predicts a Muon contraction coefficient proportional to B ​ p \sqrt{Bp} , compared with SGD’s linear dependence on the local frequency scale p p . Orthogonal equivariance differs from coordinatewise sign updates. We use SignSGD as a proxy for Adam’s coordinatewise adaptivity ( Balles and Hennig, 2018 ; Kunstner et al., 2023 ) . Muon is orthogonally equivariant whereas SignSGD is basis dependent. In a two-task rotated sparse-support construction, a batch containing only the frequent task leaves the rare-task Muon margin unchanged but can decrease the corresponding SignSGD margin under certain conditions.

We study when Muon’s preconditioning benefits survive stochastic gradient noise. Under isotropic low-SNR noise, its first-order conditional mean update matches learning-rate-rescaled SGD, showing that samplewise spectral normalization alone does not guarantee directional preconditioning. Structured sampling yields richer behavior: we establish an exact two-task balancing threshold and analyze higher-rank sampling effects governed by B ​ p j Bp_{j} . Label noise further separates task coverage from gradient reliability; an isotropic covariance closure with a locally homogeneous frequency approximation predicts square-root frequency dependence near the noisy optimum. A separate momentum-free SignSGD comparison highlights Muon’s protection against rotation-induced negative transfer under sparse sampling. Our momentum analysis connects frozen-state variance reduction with local tracking error, motivating longer memory for rare, slowly varying directions. This provides a sampling-based interpretation of heterogeneous momentum designs, supported by a preliminary 0.12B pretraining experiment in which fast–slow momentum lowers validation loss relative to Muon. Extending the analysis to evolving, non-orthogonal representations and validating these benefits across training scales remain important directions.

2610.30676:131eaa5736940c8c55870544e58d8.question: Across the five Llama and Qwen models, how do post-hoc singular-value smoothing and spiking of up_proj and down_proj affect measured task quality? What unperturbed and random-perturbation controls, intervention strengths, and uncertainty estimates support a causal interpretation?

passages.text: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches these deviations, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller relative to the geometric mean (spiking); and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness/hallucination/safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

(a) Schematic illustration of the singular-value perturbation applied to feed-forward projection matrices. (b) Trait-level response profiles under spectral perturbation, showing how behavior shifts across models and perturbation strengths. (c) Selected task-level outcomes, highlighting that the same perturbation can improve some subtasks while degrading others. Figure 1: Overview of the perturbation setup and representative behavioral effects. Panel (a) visualizes the SVD-based perturbation schema, panel (b) summarizes trait-level responses, and panel (c) highlights selective task-level changes induced by the intervention. Large language model behavior is usually analyzed through prompting, finetuning, or activation-level interventions. By contrast, we ask whether a small, interpretable change to pretrained weight spectra is already enough to expose structure in downstream behavior. The singular values of transformer MLP projections summarize how strongly each layer amplifies different directions; if that spectral geometry carries functional information, then changing it in a controlled way should produce at least partly systematic behavioral effects rather than only unstructured noise. We therefore study a constrained intervention on feed-forward projections in which singular values are reweighted around their geometric mean while the corresponding singular vectors are left unchanged. This makes spectral inequality itself the manipulated variable and lets us ask whether broad capability patterns can be reorganized without changing tokenization, prompts, or optimization. Figure 1 previews the three complementary views used throughout the paper: the intervention itself, broad behavioral shifts, and concrete task-level gains and losses.

The empirical picture that emerges is not one of uniform quality loss. Instead, spectral smoothing and spiking redistribute behavior across benchmark modules, auxiliary tasks, and personality-style probes. Some settings mainly suppress language and deductive responses, while others preserve or even improve specific factual or task-local behaviors. The goal of the paper is therefore not to identify a universally best α \alpha , but to characterize which capabilities become more or less available under controlled spectral perturbation. Our main contributions are threefold: • We introduce a lightweight singular-value smoothing/spiking intervention for transformer MLP projections and evaluate it across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . • We build a subtask-level capability-response analysis over 118 subtasks, using a retained three-dimensional basis of Factual Knowledge , Language Understanding , and Deductive Reasoning . • We provide evidence that spectral perturbations induce non-uniform tradeoffs across capability-labeled benchmark modules, auxiliary tasks, judge-scored truthfulness/hallucination/safety evaluations, and TRAIT personality probes ( Lee et al., 2024 ) , and we relate this heterogeneity to non-uniform layerwise spectral sensitivity.

Even with those limits, the intervention is attractive because it is post-hoc, architecture-aware, and easy to audit. The results motivate future variants such as layer-normalized α \alpha , projection-specific controls for up_proj and down_proj , or expert-wise safeguards for MoE models. More broadly, they suggest that weight-space spectral statistics are a useful handle for probing how different capabilities are bundled together in large language models.

The Gini plot shows that spectral inequality differs substantially by layer, model, and projection. Dense Llama models exhibit strong depth dependence, especially in up_proj ; Qwen3 8B has unusually concentrated early layers; and Qwen3 30B-A3B MoE adds expert-level variation, where the maximum expert can deviate substantially from the layer mean. The relative top-singular-value plot identifies where the same global perturbation causes the largest multiplicative amplification or suppression, with the strongest effects occurring in layers whose top singular value is already far above the geometric mean. Model / proj. Layer Base Gini Top-SV multiplier Qwen3 8B / down_proj 1 0.3209 1.7984 Qwen3 8B / down_proj 2 0.3513 1.7278 Llama 3.2 3B Instruct / up_proj 27 0.2506 1.6784 Llama 3.1 8B Instruct / up_proj 31 0.2143 1.6535 Qwen3 8B / up_proj 2 0.3910 1.6443 Table 9: Examples of large top-singular-value amplification at α = + 0.2 \alpha=+0.2 . These cases illustrate that the same global perturbation can produce markedly different realized updates across layers.

Using one global α \alpha remains useful as a controlled intervention, but it should be interpreted as a spectrum-dependent perturbation rather than a uniform update. This explains why α \alpha sweeps can produce selective task improvements or degradations rather than smooth global quality changes. The layer-wise diagnostics motivate safer future variants such as layer-normalized α \alpha , projection-specific α \alpha for up_proj and down_proj , MoE expert clipping, and reporting realized spectral statistics alongside the nominal α \alpha value.

selections.summary: Develops a singular-learning-theory account of LoRA’s non-identifiable factorization. Under local linearization, a forward-backward covariance determines which low-rank updates are statistically observable; numerical experiments examine layer-dependent geometry.
selections.relevance: A strong conceptual match for LoRA geometry, though the inspected evidence does not establish practical fine-tuning gains.

evidence.quote: Under a local linearization of the pretrained network, we show that LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback–Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance.

Numerical experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.

limitations: No strong paper on optimizer-state compression or low-rank-gradient pretraining emerged from the focused searches of this fixed corpus.
S-SALAAD’s cited memory and throughput measurements concern deployment inference; comparable training-resource costs remain unresolved in the retrieved passages.
The Muon paper’s transformer run is a diagnostic, not evidence that its proposed mechanism improves LLM training against AdamW.
The agent-harness result comes from a geochemistry simulator, so transfer to paper-digest workflows is untested here.
Repository availability and reproducibility were not verified. X analysis was disabled.

Evaluate tradeoffs among model quality, memory, throughput, and communication cost across model scales.
Build an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness.

Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. candidates.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network.
